Mr Wickham makes a much better, more charming impression, than Mr Darcy. He acts as a barrier between the two because of his charm, but also because of his longstanding feud with Mr Darcy.

Elizabeth is charmed by his demeanour and his self-deprecating nature. He acts as a kind of foil to Mr Darcy, who is closed off and prideful. Mr Wickham becomes the charming figure that Elizabeth is drawn to, further cementing his status as the barrier between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy. Later, it is because of Mr Wickham that Elizabeth realises her growing attraction to Mr Darcy, especially when he begins to help her family out of a problematic situation Mr Wickham put them in.

This scene is very important because it sets up the later scandal between Lydia and Mr Wickham, where Mr Wickham runs away with Lydia to elope, which has the potential to ruin the marriage prospects of her sisters. Elizabeth is charmed by his offer to buy her sister a ribbon, but Lydia is even more charmed by his actions. The potential ruin for her family creates the moment of ritual death between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth, because Elizabeth was finally starting to see Mr Darcy in a more favourable light. When she learns her sister intends to elope, she realises it will be a stain on her reputation, that could prevent Mr Darcy from being allowed to marry her.

The tense moment between Mr Wickham and Mr Darcy reveals their longstanding dislike of each other, especially the moment where Mr Darcy gallops away on his horse. Elizabeth interprets it as Mr Darcy being rude and dismissive of Mr Wickham, instead of Mr Darcy's anger at Mr Wickham's being around more young ladies he has the opportunity to ruin.

Mr Wickham's refusal to leave is ironic, because he does actually avoid attending the ball. He avoids Mr Darcy, because a confrontation would expose his previous behaviour, and clue the Bennett family into his actions. By talking of his hatred of Mr Darcy, he further cements the barrier between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy, as Mr Wickham has become someone she trusts. He doesn't tell her the full truth, however, and when she does uncover the truth of what Mr Wickham has done, she immediately turns against him - especially when he tries something similar with her sister, Lydia.

The barrier between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy is at its strongest after this moment. Mr Wickham has mislead her into believing that Mr Darcy stole from him, instead of that he gambled away his money, and then attempted to elope with Mr Darcy's sister. Once the barrier is dismantled (the truth comes out), Elizabeth has fewer reasons to dislike Mr Darcy, and instead slowly comes to admire him for his actions in defending his sister.

Mr Darcy cannot help but constantly be drawn to Elizabeth. He seems to always know exactly where she is in a room. It really makes his attraction to Elizabeth seem very obvious - to everyone, expect Elizabeth.

Elizabeth tries to get some breathing room from Mr Darcy and goes for a walk. Mr Darcy follows her, because he can deny his feelings no longer. This is his moment of declaration - in a way, there are two moments of declaration in each romance book. Each party of the relationship must eventually recognise and confess their feelings. At the moment of Mr Darcy's declaration, Elizabeth doesn't possess the same feelings. It takes time for her to realise what she actually feels for him.

This is Mr Darcy's moment of declaration. He says he only came to Rosings to see Elizabeth, because he couldn't bear to be parted from her. It is a romantic sentiment, but his wording could use some work. For Mr Darcy, this is the culmination of all the weeks of yearning since he first met Elizabeth. He has spent plenty of time getting to know her, being around her, and finding her irresistible. For Elizabeth, this moment comes completely out of the blue, because she believed he barely tolerated her presence - instead, he's saying he seeks her out. Her bafflement at his declaration is genuinely the only response that makes sense for her character.

Mr Darcy insists on reminding them both of the multitude of barriers that should prevent them from being together, before he declares that his feelings continue to exist despite everything. It makes his declaration sound moire like a list of insults than a confession of love.

Elizabeth's pride is rather offended by Mr Darcy's declaration. For Mr Darcy, it is this moment that acts as a kind of moment of ritual death. It prevents the romance he had envisioned from happening, because Elizabeth has less-than-politely rejected his proposal.

This scene sparks the moment of recognition between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth, and also provides Mr Darcy a roadmap for earning Elizabeth's affection. It also opens Elizabeth's eyes to the behaviour of her own family members, and she begins to realise that Mr Darcy wasn't as arrogant as he may have appeared, and that her family is at times, rather improper. Their communication during this scene helps them both to understand the situation better. They are both better able to understand the errors in their actions. Mr Darcy learns that Elizabeth's family is very important to her, and Elizabeth learns that Mr Darcy wanted to protect his friend from being taken advantage of.

The moment of ritual death continues when Elizabeth mentions Mr Wickham, which sparks that protective instinct in Mr Darcy to cover up what almost happened to cast ruin upon his younger sister. It causes him to further insult Elizabeth, leading to her outright rejection of his proposal. His relationship with Mr Wickham is another obstacle between him and Elizabeth, and once he has recovered from his hurt, he quickly addresses this misunderstanding. The explanation of what actually happened does create more attraction between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy, leading them towards their moment of recognition, when they are finally in the same place in their relationship.

Elizabeth is so overwhelmed by everything that Mr Darcy has done for Elizabeth and her family that she cannot sleep. She goes for a morning walk instead, and comes across Mr Darcy. There are no longer any issues or barriers preventing them from being together, so it's time for a betrothal.

Elizabeth apologising for her behaviour and harsh judgement is what gives Mr Darcy hope that her feelings have changed, leading him to attempt another betrothal. Mr Darcy also confesses that everything he's done was for her, proving his feelings are more than just words.

The betrothal scene also contains a declaration of love from Mr Darcy. He expresses his hopes for their future, but also gives Elizabeth the opportunity to back away, especially after his last proposal went quite badly. This time, the proposal is accepted - not in as many words, but there is something beautiful in their quiet moment together.

Lady Catherine's arrival acts as another moment of ritual death, because it cements that a woman of high standing doesn't believe Elizabeth is a good fit for Mr Darcy. Elizabeth's interaction with Lady Catherine also becomes Elizabeth's declaration of feeling.

Lady Catherine's determination to come between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy reinforces the barrier of class, acting as a kind of moment of ritual death. However, Elizabeth is aware of the class system, and knows that Mr Darcy has the right to choose to wed any woman he pleases. Lady Catherine's objections relate to her plans to marry her own daughter to Mr Darcy, who she believes is a better match for him than Elizabeth.

Elizabeth's defensiveness against Lady Catherine acts as a declaration. If she was uninterested in Mr Darcy's proposal, she simply could have refuted the rumours, and Lady Catherine would have been on her way. Instead, her choice to argue with Lady Catherine implies that she would be interested in a proposal, if one were to occur. She does not mention that she has already refused Mr Darcy's proposal, because she has made the decision that she would accept if he were to ask again. Especially after all he has done for her family.

Through the very implication that Mr Darcy is engaged to her daughter, Elizabeth tears down Lady Catherine's argument. She and Lady Catherine both know Mr Darcy has the right to choose whom he will marry, regardless of Lady Catherine's designs. It acts as a declaration of Elizabeth's feelings, and also brings Elizabeth and Mr Darcy into a moment of recognition. They are finally in the same place, with the same feelings.

Elizabeth confessing that she is not engaged to Mr Darcy is a little bit of a return to their moment of ritual death. It's a reminder to her that she's already turned down his proposal, and potentially destroyed any chance for the future she now desperately wants. When Lady Catherine demands she promise to turn down any proposal, she refuses. That moment is the moment that signals to Mr Darcy that perhaps, Elizabeth's feelings towards him have changed.

Lydia's elopement ending in a wedding has prevented the family from entering into a scandal, but Elizabeth is still furious that it is being brushed under the rug, and Lydia does not seem to be facing consequences. The scandal is still enough that it could lower the reputation of her sisters.

Lydia is still unaware of the potential damage she could have wreaked on the family's reputation. Elizabeth is frustrated, because her sister came between her and Mr Darcy, and since news of her elopement came, she hasn't heard from Mr Darcy. She has started to believe that Mr Darcy has abandoned his pursuit of her.

This is the moment where Elizabeth's feelings for Mr Darcy become confirmed. She now realises that instead of pursuing her, he went to help her sister, and prevent the scandal from affecting Elizabeth's entire family. He wasn't avoiding Elizabeth because of the scandal, he was actively attempting to minimise its effects. Elizabeth realises what Mr Darcy is willing to do to help her. It also resolves the moment of ritual death, because it becomes clear to Elizabeth that Mr Darcy never intended to abandon her just because of the elopement - he ran off to fix things.

Elizabeth makes clear her feelings towards Mr Wickham by ignoring him. Her family could have easily been ruined by his actions, and she hasn't forgotten what Mr Darcy told her about him either. Mr Wickham's actions have only cemented her good opinion of Mr Darcy.

This clip introduces one of the barriers between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy, which is Elizabeth's dismissal of the men of society. She does not believe they are worth her time.

This scene includes the introduction of Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley to society. The way the crowd falls silent and the music stops indicates the importance of the pair. Elizabeth, Jane and Charlotte discuss Mr Darcy's wealth, to further establish the barrier of social class.
A brief meeting of eyes between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy, where Mr Darcy appears briefly shocked to have noticed Elizabeth, and Elizabeth seems a little pleased to have captured his attention.
Further establishes society with Mrs Bennett being eager to introduce her daughters to the two eligible men, in hopes of securing a prosperous marriage for them.

The first official meeting between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth. The ball continues, Jane and Mr Bingley have their first conversation. Further defines society, and begins to set up a barrier between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth. Mr Darcy doesn't approve of the match between Jane and Mr Bingley because of her family's inappropriate behaviour within society.

The arrival of the officers to town also presents another barrier between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth in the form of Mr Wickham. He will become the heart of a misunderstanding between them, and also the heart of the moment of ritual death.

When Jane and Mr Bingley begin dancing, Mr Darcy and Elizabeth are left standing together at the side of the room. Elizabeth seems rather hurt by his clipped response, especially after she was slightly delighted by his attention earlier. His coldness towards her contributes to the barrier of her believing he is unfeeling toward her.

Elizabeth overhears a conversation between Mr Bingley and Mr Darcy where Mr Darcy refers to her as "tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me" and she is offended. This contributes to the barrier, because Elizabeth struggles to forget his assessment of her, and her pride prevents her from ignoring it.
Charlotte and Jane mock Mr Darcy, and Jane decides he is the last man she would ever dance with. This becomes relevant when she says a similar thing to Mr Darcy during his proposal.
Mr Darcy broods in the corner while everyone else has a lovely time dancing. He doesn't tend to engage with society, which is another point against him in Elizabeth's books.

Mr Darcy helps Mr Bingley practice his proposal to Jane. This helps tear down the very last barrier, and officially ends the moment of ritual death. With the engagement of Jane and Mr Bingley, all of Elizabeth's reasons for objecting to Mr Darcy's proposal are null and void.

Mr Bingley proposes to Jane, which officially dismantles the last reason Elizabeth has for rejecting Mr Darcy's proposal. After this scene, the moment of ritual death is officially over, and there is nothing of merit standing between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy.

Mr Darcy's attraction to Elizabeth is undeniable. Every time she enters the room, all of his attention is immediately focused on her. She feels rather uncomfortable from his attention, because she doesn't understand what it means.

This scene is more an example of the barrier than of Mr Darcys attraction. In this scene, he comes across as rather arrogant and demanding. The closes he gets to showing a sign of his attraction to Elizabeth is at the end, where he suggests an accomplished woman should open her mind by reading, and Elizabeth closes her book immediately.

This scene is a callback to the first ball Elizabeth and Mr Darcy both attended, where she asked if he danced and he said "not if I can help it." His decision to ask her to dance explores the attraction he feels for her in a very subtle way. It makes it clear that though he dislikes dancing, he would happily dance with her. His lack of expression could be interpreted as dismissive formality (which is likely how Elizabeth sees it) but it could also be interpreted as nerves. Elizabeth is completely shocked at this turn of events, because she is still acting under the assumption that he doesn't like her. He has not done the best job of showing her his interest. His decision to ask Elizabeth to dance is his announcement of his feelings and regard for her, but she doesn't pick up on that.

Mr Darcy's attraction becomes more obvious each time he and Elizabeth are in a room with other people. Mr Darcy only really seems to have attention for her, and he completely ignores Mr Collins in order to address Elizabeth.

Another example of Mr Darcy ignoring most polite social conventions by abandoning a conversation so he could spend time staring at Elizabeth while she plays piano. Mr Darcy's implication that he couldn't alarm Elizabeth even if he wanted to suggests that he is intrigued by the way she doesn't care about his thoughts. He is intrigued by her self-assuredness.

Elizabeth making fun of Mr Darcy's behaviour at the first ball continues to ensure Mr Darcy is aware of the little regard she has for him. He feels the need to defend his actions, but Elizabeth is quick to dismiss his defence. Mr Darcy feels the need to improve her impression of him, because he wants her to think as highly of him as he does of her.

Elizabeth reminds Mr Darcy that self-improvement is an option he possesses. That's why at the next ball, he is quick to ask her to dance. He thinks it will improve her perception of him. He is following the guidance she gives him. He also makes it clear that he is trying to converse with her now.

It's almost like he was building up to propose and then changed his mind. He ignores Charlotte, the lady of the house, on his exit. It makes it very clear he was there to see Elizabeth, and only Elizabeth.

Mr Darcy's first proposal... needs some work. But his attraction is undeniable, especially when he chronologically lists all the reasons he shouldn't be marrying her, and implies that he simply must anyway, because he loves her so much. Poor Elizabeth is completely bamboozled.

Elizabeth is feeling very awkward when she encounters Mr Darcy during a visit to his estate. In a way, this is when Elizabeth starts to feel attracted to Mr Darcy, through the exploration of his estate, she realises what she'd given up when she rejected his proposal. He further cements her regretting of the rejection when he supports his family, but this scene marks a turning point for Elizabeth.

Elizabeth's attraction to Mr Darcy grows when she sees the way he acts around his sister. He is basically a whole different person. She also realises just how deeply Mr Darcy's feelings must go, if he spends so much time talking about Elizabeth to his sister.

This scene is the moment of recognition, where they're both in a place to realise the full extent of their feelings for each other. It is also the moment of Elizabeth's declaration. She finally realises just how much he has been trying to help her and her family. That, more than anything else, endears him to her.

The proposal scene! This is where the attraction is most evident, because it's the resolution of the film. It's also the moment of recognition, where both characters agree to enter into a relationship together, despite any obstacles they may face.

Elizabeth is feeling rather out of sorts after Mr Darcy's proposal to her. It's almost like she's grieving the life she could had led, if Mr Darcy were a more tolerable version of himself. She also doesn't feel much like being out in society because she doesn't want to risk encountering Mr Darcy. She is also beginning to slowly realise he was right about everything he said, and she was quite harsh. He is about to dismantle the last argument she had, which was his dislike of Mr Wickham, through the letter.

Mr Darcy will not attempt to talk her into marriage, but he does wish to defend his own honour. This is where the barrier is torn down quite well. Elizabeth is no longer able to hold Mr Darcy away after she reads the letter. The removal of the barrier allows her to see who Mr Darcy really is, and allows her attraction to him to grow over the course of the film. She is then only able to judge him on his actions, and her own perceptions.

Mr Darcy's letter explaining his dislike of Mr Wickham is the final barrier removal between him and Elizabeth. His defence of his sister also endears him to Elizabeth, because it's the kind of thing she would do for her family. She starts to recognise that he might have a reason for his actions, and begins to search for those reasons, instead of making assumptions. His love for his sister is one of the things that kindles the start of Elizabeth's developing attraction to Mr Darcy.

The second part of Mr Darcy's letter addresses his actions in preventing the union between Jane and Mr Bingley. He explains that he thought what he was doing was in defence of his friend. It assists Elizabeth in realising that Mr Darcy is steadfastly loyal to those he loves, which is a trait Jane also shares - even if they are both a little blind in their defence of their families.

Another example of Mr Darcy ignoring most polite social conventions by abandoning a conversation so he could spend time staring at Elizabeth while she plays piano. It causes him to further insult Elizabeth, leading to her outright rejection of his proposal. His relationship with Mr Wickham is another obstacle between him and Elizabeth, and once he has recovered from his hurt, he quickly addresses this misunderstanding. The explanation of what actually happened does create more attraction between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy, leading them towards their moment of recognition, when they are finally in the same place in their relationship.

Elizabeth is so overwhelmed by everything that Mr Darcy has done for Elizabeth and her family that she cannot sleep. She goes for a morning walk instead, and comes across Mr Darcy. There are no longer any issues or barriers preventing them from being together, so it's time for a betrothal.

Elizabeth apologising for her behaviour and harsh judgement is what gives Mr Darcy hope that her feelings have changed, leading him to attempt another betrothal. Mr Darcy also confesses that everything he's done was for her, proving his feelings are more than just words.

The betrothal scene also contains a declaration of love from Mr Darcy. He expresses his hopes for their future, but also gives Elizabeth the opportunity to back away, especially after his last proposal went quite badly. This time, the proposal is accepted - not in as many words, but there is something beautiful in their quiet moment together.

Lady Catherine's arrival acts as another moment of ritual death, because it cements that a woman of high standing doesn't believe Elizabeth is a good fit for Mr Darcy. Elizabeth's interaction with Lady Catherine also becomes Elizabeth's declaration of feeling.

Lady Catherine's determination to come between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy reinforces the barrier of class, acting as a kind of moment of ritual death. However, Elizabeth is aware of the class system, and knows that Mr Darcy has the right to choose to wed any woman he pleases. Lady Catherine's objections relate to her plans to marry her own daughter to Mr Darcy, who she believes is a better match for him than Elizabeth.

Elizabeth's defensiveness against Lady Catherine acts as a declaration. If she was uninterested in Mr Darcy's proposal, she simply could have refuted the rumours, and Lady Catherine would have been on her way. Instead, her choice to argue with Lady Catherine implies that she would be interested in a proposal, if one were to occur. She does not mention that she has already refused Mr Darcy's proposal, because she has made the decision that she would accept if he were to ask again. Especially after all he has done for her family.

Through the very implication that Mr Darcy is engaged to her daughter, Elizabeth tears down Lady Catherine's argument. She and Lady Catherine both know Mr Darcy has the right to choose whom he will marry, regardless of Lady Catherine's designs. It acts as a declaration of Elizabeth's feelings, and also brings Elizabeth and Mr Darcy into a moment of recognition. They are finally in the same place, with the same feelings.

Elizabeth confessing that she is not engaged to Mr Darcy is a little bit of a return to their moment of ritual death. It's a reminder to her that she's already turned down his proposal, and potentially destroyed any chance for the future she now desperately wants. When Lady Catherine demands she promise to turn down any proposal, she refuses. That moment is the moment that signals to Mr Darcy that perhaps, Elizabeth's feelings towards him have changed.

Lydia's elopement ending in a wedding has prevented the family from entering into a scandal, but Elizabeth is still furious that it is being brushed under the rug, and Lydia does not seem to be facing consequences. The scandal is still enough that it could lower the reputation of her sisters.

Lydia is still unaware of the potential damage she could have wreaked on the family's reputation. Elizabeth is frustrated, because her sister came between her and Mr Darcy, and since news of her elopement came, she hasn't heard from Mr Darcy. She has started to believe that Mr Darcy has abandoned his pursuit of her.

This is the moment where Elizabeth's feelings for Mr Darcy become confirmed. She now realises that instead of pursuing her, he went to help her sister, and prevent the scandal from affecting Elizabeth's entire family. He wasn't avoiding Elizabeth because of the scandal, he was actively attempting to minimise its effects. Elizabeth realises what Mr Darcy is willing to do to help her. It also resolves the moment of ritual death, because it becomes clear to Elizabeth that Mr Darcy never intended to abandon her just because of the elopement - he ran off to fix things.

Elizabeth makes clear her feelings towards Mr Wickham by ignoring him. Her family could have easily been ruined by his actions, and she hasn't forgotten what Mr Darcy told her about him either. Mr Wickham's actions have only cemented her good opinion of Mr Darcy.

The film starts with the introduction of society. Elizabeth and her sister Jane are sitting down at the ball, watching the dancing happening around them as they talk about the men in the room. This clip introduces one of the barriers between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy, which is Elizabeth's dismissal of the men of society. She does not believe they are worth her time.

This scene includes the introduction of Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley to society. The way the crowd falls silent and the music stops indicates the importance of the pair. Elizabeth, Jane and Charlotte discuss Mr Darcy's wealth, to further establish the barrier of social class.
A brief meeting of eyes between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy, where Mr Darcy appears briefly shocked to have noticed Elizabeth, and Elizabeth seems a little pleased to have captured his attention.
Further establishes society with Mrs Bennett being eager to introduce her daughters to the two eligible men, in hopes of securing a prosperous marriage for them.

The first official meeting between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth. Mr Darcy continues to focus his attention mostly on Elizabeth, but seems bored by the whole affair, as he doesn't much enjoy the performance of society. He is also irritated by the behaviour of Mrs Bennett in this scene, because of the way she is attempting to foist her daughters off on the wealthy men.

The ball continues, Jane and Mr Bingley have their first conversation. Further defines society, and begins to set up a barrier between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth. Mr Darcy doesn't approve of the match between Jane and Mr Bingley because of her family's inappropriate behaviour within society.

The arrival of the officers to town also presents another barrier between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth in the form of Mr Wickham. He will become the heart of a misunderstanding between them, and also the heart of the moment of ritual death.

When Jane and Mr Bingley begin dancing, Mr Darcy and Elizabeth are left standing together at the side of the room. This leads to one of their more awkward interactions, where Mr Darcy refuses to dance with Elizabeth, despite their being a lack of men in the room (this is evidenced by a later clip where Elizabeth dances with Charlotte). Elizabeth seems rather hurt by his clipped response, especially after she was slightly delighted by his attention earlier. His coldness towards her contributes to the barrier of her believing he is unfeeling toward her.

Elizabeth overhears a conversation between Mr Bingley and Mr Darcy where Mr Darcy refers to her as "tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me" and she is offended. This contributes to the barrier, because Elizabeth struggles to forget his assessment of her, and her pride prevents her from ignoring it.
Charlotte and Jane mock Mr Darcy, and Jane decides he is the last man she would ever dance with. This becomes relevant when she says a similar thing to Mr Darcy during his proposal.
Mr Darcy broods in the corner while everyone else has a lovely time dancing. He doesn't tend to engage with society, which is another point against him in Elizabeth's books.

This is the moment of ritual death. Elizabeth and Mr Darcy had been developing a kind of friendship after Elizabeth's visit to Pemberley House. The news of Lydia's elopement destroys that relationship they'd been building, because if Lydia doesn't go through with the elopement, her family's reputation will be destroyed. This would prevent Mr Darcy from being able to marry Elizabeth. It seems to be an impenetrable obstacle to their relationship.

Both Mr Darcy and Elizabeth are realising the severity of the situation. Mr Darcy blames himself for not preventing Mr Wickham from attempting to elope with another girl, and Elizabeth blames herself for not warning her sister's of Mr Wickham's behaviour. They're both devastated at their lack of intervention, especially when they consdier what it means for their own relationship.

This dialogue between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy is as thinly veiled a confession they can make. Elizabeth says they've run out of time, and there's nothing they can do. She is mourning her relationship with Mr Darcy. Mr Darcy is planning how he can intervene to prevent ruin from falling on Elizabeth's family. He is trying to protect what she values.

Mr Darcy leaves, and Elizabeth's uncle leaves, so they can attempt to find Lydia before the family is ruined. Elizabeth doesn't know what Mr Darcy intends to do, and may believe he is attempting to distance himself from her before the scandal breaks.

Mr Darcy helps Mr Bingley practice his proposal to Jane. This helps tear down the very last barrier, and officially ends the moment of ritual death. With the engagement of Jane and Mr Bingley, all of Elizabeth's reasons for objecting to Mr Darcy's proposal are null and void.
Elizabeth finally begins to declare to her sister that her feelings towards Mr Darcy have changed, and this is before she knows Mr Darcy is actively trying to reconcile her sister and Mr Bingley.

Mr Bingley proposes to Jane, which officially dismantles the last reason Elizabeth has for rejecting Mr Darcy's proposal. After this scene, the moment of ritual death is officially over, and there is nothing of merit standing between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy.
Mr Darcy's first glimpse of Elizabeth Bennett. It becomes very clear that he's attracted to her just from that quick glance, and then he studiously avoids eye contact.

Mr Darcy's attraction to Elizabeth is undeniable. Every time she enters the room, all of his attention is immediately focused on her. She feels rather uncomfortable from his attention, because she doesn't understand what it means.

This scene is more an example of the barrier than of Mr Darcys attraction. In this scene, he comes across as rather arrogant and demanding. The closes he gets to showing a sign of his attraction to Elizabeth is at the end, where he suggests an accomplished woman should open her mind by reading, and Elizabeth closes her book immediately.

Mr Darcy helping Elizabeth into the carriage is one of the most recognisable scenes from the film. It is where his attraction to Elizabeth becomes the most obvious. The way he flexes his hand, like he's trying to remember what it felt like to hold her hand.

This scene is a callback to the first ball Elizabeth and Mr Darcy both attended, where she asked if he danced and he said "not if I can help it." His decision to ask her to dance explores the attraction he feels for her in a very subtle way. It makes it clear that though he dislikes dancing, he would happily dance with her. His lack of expression could be interpreted as dismissive formality (which is likely how Elizabeth sees it) but it could also be interpreted as nerves. Elizabeth is completely shocked at this turn of events, because she is still acting under the assumption that he doesn't like her. He has not done the best job of showing her his interest. His decision to ask Elizabeth to dance is his announcement of his feelings and regard for her, but she doesn't pick up on that.

Mr Darcy's attraction becomes more obvious each time he and Elizabeth are in a room with other people. Mr Darcy only really seems to have attention for her, and he completely ignores Mr Collins in order to address Elizabeth.

Another example of Mr Darcy ignoring most polite social conventions by abandoning a conversation so he could spend time staring at Elizabeth while she plays piano. Mr Darcy's implication that he couldn't alarm Elizabeth even if he wanted to suggests that he is intrigued by the way she doesn't care about his thoughts. He is intrigued by her self-assuredness.

Elizabeth making fun of Mr Darcy's behaviour at the first ball continues to ensure Mr Darcy is aware of the little regard she has for him. He feels the need to defend his actions, but Elizabeth is quick to dismiss his defence. Mr Darcy feels the need to improve her impression of him, because he wants her to think as highly of him as he does of her.

Elizabeth reminds Mr Darcy that self-improvement is an option he possesses. That's why at the next ball, he is quick to ask her to dance. He thinks it will improve her perception of him. He is following the guidance she gives him. He also makes it clear that he is trying to converse with her now.

Mr Darcy wanted an excuse to visit Elizabeth, and then forgot what his excuse was upon arrival. His attraction (or at the very least, his desire to be in Elizabeth's presence) is very obvious in this scene. He came upon a reason to visit her, and then immediately left upon interruption. It's almost like he was building up to propose and then changed his mind. He ignores Charlotte, the lady of the house, on his exit. It makes it very clear he was there to see Elizabeth, and only Elizabeth.

Mr Darcy's first proposal... needs some work. But his attraction is undeniable, especially when he chronologically lists all the reasons he shouldn't be marrying her, and implies that he simply must anyway, because he loves her so much. Poor Elizabeth is completely bamboozled.

Elizabeth is feeling very awkward when she encounters Mr Darcy during a visit to his estate. In a way, this is when Elizabeth starts to feel attracted to Mr Darcy, through the exploration of his estate, she realises what she'd given up when she rejected his proposal. He further cements her regretting of the rejection when he supports his family, but this scene marks a turning point for Elizabeth.

Elizabeth's attraction to Mr Darcy grows when she sees the way he acts around his sister. He is basically a whole different person. She also realises just how deeply Mr Darcy's feelings must go, if he spends so much time talking about Elizabeth to his sister.

This scene is the moment of recognition, where they're both in a place to realise the full extent of their feelings for each other. It is also the moment of Elizabeth's declaration. She finally realises just how much he has been trying to help her and her family. That, more than anything else, endears him to her.

The proposal scene! This is where the attraction is most evident, because it's the resolution of the film. It's also the moment of recognition, where both characters agree to enter into a relationship together, despite any obstacles they may face.

Elizabeth is feeling rather out of sorts after Mr Darcy's proposal to her. It's almost like she's grieving the life she could had led, if Mr Darcy were a more tolerable version of himself. She also doesn't feel much like being out in society because she doesn't want to risk encountering Mr Darcy. She is also beginning to slowly realise he was right about everything he said, and she was quite harsh. He is about to dismantle the last argument she had, which was his dislike of Mr Wickham, through the letter.

Mr Darcy will not attempt to talk her into marriage, but he does wish to defend his own honour. This is where the barrier is torn down quite well. Elizabeth is no longer able to hold Mr Darcy away after she reads the letter. The removal of the barrier allows her to see who Mr Darcy really is, and allows her attraction to him to grow over the course of the film. She is then only able to judge him on his actions, and her own perceptions.

Mr Darcy's letter explaining his dislike of Mr Wickham is the final barrier removal between him and Elizabeth. His defence of his sister also endears him to Elizabeth, because it's the kind of thing she would do for her family. She starts to recognise that he might have a reason for his actions, and begins to search for those reasons, instead of making assumptions. His love for his sister is one of the things that kindles the start of Elizabeth's developing attraction to Mr Darcy.

The second part of Mr Darcy's letter addresses his actions in preventing the union between Jane and Mr Bingley. He explains that he thought what he was doing was in defence of his friend. It assists Elizabeth in realising that Mr Darcy is steadfastly loyal to those he loves, which is a trait Jane also shares - even if they are both a little blind in their defence of their families.
The arrival of the officers portends the arrival of Mr Wickham, who acts as a barrier between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy.

Mr Wickham picking up the handkerchief for Elizabeth initiates the start of their relationship, and acts as their initial "meeting". Mr Wickham makes a much better, more charming impression, than Mr Darcy. He acts as a barrier between the two because of his charm, but also because of his longstanding feud with Mr Darcy.

Elizabeth is charmed by his demeanour and his self-deprecating nature. He acts as a kind of foil to Mr Darcy, who is closed off and prideful. Mr Wickham becomes the charming figure that Elizabeth is drawn to, further cementing his status as the barrier between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy. Later, it is because of Mr Wickham that Elizabeth realises her growing attraction to Mr Darcy, especially when he begins to help her family out of a problematic situation Mr Wickham put them in.

This scene is very important because it sets up the later scandal between Lydia and Mr Wickham, where Mr Wickham runs away with Lydia to elope, which has the potential to ruin the marriage prospects of her sisters. Elizabeth is charmed by his offer to buy her sister a ribbon, but Lydia is even more charmed by his actions. The potential ruin for her family creates the moment of ritual death between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth, because Elizabeth was finally starting to see Mr Darcy in a more favourable light. When she learns her sister intends to elope, she realises it will be a stain on her reputation, that could prevent Mr Darcy from being allowed to marry her.

The tense moment between Mr Wickham and Mr Darcy reveals their longstanding dislike of each other, especially the moment where Mr Darcy gallops away on his horse. Elizabeth interprets it as Mr Darcy being rude and dismissive of Mr Wickham, instead of Mr Darcy's anger at Mr Wickham's being around more young ladies he has the opportunity to ruin.

Mr Wickham's refusal to leave is ironic, because he does actually avoid attending the ball. He avoids Mr Darcy, because a confrontation would expose his previous behaviour, and clue the Bennett family into his actions. By talking of his hatred of Mr Darcy, he further cements the barrier between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy, as Mr Wickham has become someone she trusts. He doesn't tell her the full truth, however, and when she does uncover the truth of what Mr Wickham has done, she immediately turns against him - especially when he tries something similar with her sister, Lydia.

The barrier between Elizabeth and Mr Darcy is at its strongest after this moment. Mr Wickham has mislead her into believing that Mr Darcy stole from him, instead of that he gambled away his money, and then attempted to elope with Mr Darcy's sister. Once the barrier is dismantled (the truth comes out), Elizabeth has fewer reasons to dislike Mr Darcy, and instead slowly comes to admire him for his actions in defending his sister.
